paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify boundaries in a sequence whose average level changes several times. A central challenge is distinguishing a systematic change from a brief spike: a large jump between neighboring observations does not necessarily mark a genuine boundary. The proposed Bayesian model selection procedure uses non-local prior distributions to help make that distinction.

The method compares explanations of the data in terms of change points, while suppressing isolated spikes that do not represent boundaries. To make the computation faster, the authors reduce the problem of finding several changes to a sequence of problems that each seek one change. This connects the broader segmentation task to simpler detection problems.

The authors establish consistency results for both the estimated number of changes and their locations under various prior distributions. These results provide theoretical support for recovering the underlying boundaries as evidence accumulates. They also compare the method with existing approaches in extensive simulations and illustrate its use with magnetic resonance imaging guided radiation therapy data.
neurips-2018-bayesian-model-selection-ap.tldr: A Bayesian boundary detector uses non-local priors to distinguish systematic mean changes from isolated spikes, with consistency guarantees and a faster sequential formulation.

paragraphs: This paper studies sentence rewriting with explicit control over textual attributes. The model receives an original sentence together with attribute labels and attempts to produce a sentence that fits both. The challenge is to satisfy the requested attributes while retaining compatible content, rather than allowing the controls to overwhelm what the original sentence says.

The authors address these requirements through two training objectives. A reconstruction loss interpolates between auto-encoding and back-translation components, supplying pressure to preserve content. An adversarial loss encourages generated sentences to match the requested attributes and resemble realistic text. Together, these objectives connect preservation of the input with the desired properties of the output.

Quantitative measurements, qualitative examples, and human evaluations show that the model generates fluent sentences that reflect the conditioning information better than prior methods. The authors also demonstrate simultaneous control of multiple attributes. This extends the task beyond adjusting one property at a time and provides evidence that several requested changes can be coordinated within a single generation process.
neurips-2018-content-preserving-text-gen.tldr: Combining reconstruction and adversarial losses enables fluent sentence rewriting that preserves compatible content while controlling multiple attributes.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a compression objective that considers both reconstruction accuracy and the distribution of reconstructed samples. It optimizes the tradeoff between bitrate and distortion while requiring outputs to follow the training-data distribution. This formulation is motivated by image compression methods that can produce reconstructions without visible artifacts even when very few bits are available.

The resulting system connects compression to generative modeling. At zero bitrate, it learns a generative model of the data, since no transmitted information identifies the particular input. At sufficiently high bitrates, it achieves perfect reconstruction. Between these endpoints, the system smoothly interpolates between generating samples from the learned distribution and faithfully reconstructing individual training samples.

The authors investigate several approximate solutions to this constrained optimization problem, including a new combination of a Wasserstein GAN and a Wasserstein Autoencoder. They provide extensive theoretical and empirical characterization of the resulting systems. The contribution is a framework for studying how realistic output distributions and fidelity to particular inputs interact as the available communication budget changes.
neurips-2018-deep-generative-models-for-.tldr: Distribution-preserving compression connects generative modeling at zero bitrate with perfect reconstruction at sufficiently high bitrates.

paragraphs: DecaProp is a neural architecture for reading comprehension, where a model must relate a question to a passage. Its main idea is to connect passage and question representations across all hierarchical levels of the network. This allows the architecture to model relationships between representations formed at different depths, giving those relationships a central role in processing.

The connections themselves are learned through attention. Instead of using standard residual skip connections, the model introduces Bidirectional Attention Connectors to build dense links throughout the network efficiently. Attention therefore serves two purposes in the design: relating the passage to the query and determining how information connects across layers.

The authors evaluate DecaProp on four challenging reading comprehension benchmarks and report state-of-the-art results on all four. Reported absolute F1 improvements over existing baselines range from 2.6% to 14.2%. These experiments support the value of combining dense connectivity with learned attention connectors, showing gains across several tested comprehension settings rather than on a single benchmark alone.
neurips-2018-densely-connected-attention.tldr: DecaProp connects passage and question representations across network depths using attention, achieving leading results on four reading comprehension benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many samples are needed to compare discrete probability distributions while satisfying differential privacy. It studies identity testing, which checks agreement with a specified distribution, and closeness testing, which compares two sampled distributions. Both problems concern distributions over k possible elements, and the analysis accounts for the privacy parameters ε and δ.

The authors derive upper and lower sample-complexity bounds. For identity testing, their algorithms are optimal across all parameter ranges. For closeness testing, they provide the first results under this privacy formulation, with optimal bounds in the sparse regime where the sample count is at most k. Their algorithms privatize existing estimators chosen for low sensitivity to changes in the data.

The paper also develops a general method for proving privacy-related lower bounds. It connects private testing to couplings between competing hypothesis classes, then combines carefully selected priors with Le Cam’s two-point theorem. This framework explains why certain sample costs cannot be avoided. The authors suggest it may also yield strong lower bounds for other private statistical tasks.
neurips-2018-differentially-private-test.tldr: The paper establishes optimal private identity-testing sample complexity and sparse-regime closeness-testing bounds, alongside a general lower-bound framework.

paragraphs: DropBlock is a regularization method designed for convolutional neural networks. Ordinary dropout removes individual activations during training, but nearby convolutional activations are spatially correlated. The authors suggest that this correlation may let information continue flowing despite individual removals, helping explain why dropout is often less effective in convolutional layers than in fully connected layers.

DropBlock instead removes activations together within a contiguous region of a feature map. This makes the disruption spatially structured. The authors find that applying it to skip connections as well as convolutional layers increases accuracy. They also find that gradually increasing the number of removed units during training improves accuracy and makes results less sensitive to hyperparameter choices.

Experiments show better convolutional-network regularization than dropout in the tested settings. On ImageNet, ResNet-50 with DropBlock reaches 78.13% accuracy, improving the baseline by more than 1.6 percentage points. On COCO object detection, RetinaNet’s Average Precision rises from 36.8% to 38.4%. These results demonstrate benefits for both image classification and detection.
neurips-2018-dropblock-a-regularization-.tldr: DropBlock removes contiguous activation regions during training and improves convolutional-network performance on image classification and object detection.

paragraphs: The paper investigates natural-gradient optimization as a way to address difficult curvature in neural-network training objectives. Such curvature can make ordinary stochastic gradient descent struggle. Natural gradients have shown promise where they can be estimated, but their convergence behavior and practical use in very large, deep networks have remained difficult to establish.

The authors derive an exact natural-gradient expression for deep linear networks, which retain pathological curvature resembling that of nonlinear networks. They obtain an analytical convergence rate showing exponential loss reduction toward the global minimum in parameter space. The expression is computationally tractable and also helps explain why some previously proposed approximations perform well in practice.

The linear-network result supplies a basis for developing natural-gradient approximations for nonlinear models. The authors explore this direction with an online natural-gradient method and report preliminary MNIST autoencoding experiments in which it outperforms SGD while retaining computational simplicity. The theoretical guarantee concerns the linear setting; the nonlinear application is supported here by preliminary experimental evidence.
neurips-2018-exact-natural-gradient-in-d.tldr: An exact natural gradient for deep linear networks yields exponential convergence and motivates a promising preliminary optimizer for nonlinear networks.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether image classifiers can benefit from using the representation already present inside JPEG compression. Conventional convolutional networks receive RGB pixels after decompression. JPEG processing contains blockwise discrete cosine transform coefficients, which describe image information in a frequency representation. The authors propose feeding those coefficients directly to a network.

The motivation is to avoid expanding compressed image information into pixels, transferring that expanded representation, and then asking early network layers to learn frequency-like processing again. To implement the idea, the authors modify libjpeg to expose DCT coefficients and adapt ResNet-50 to the resulting input sizes and strides. The representation change therefore includes corresponding changes to the network’s input processing.

ImageNet experiments identify networks that are both faster and more accurate, as well as configurations with approximately the same accuracy as ResNet-50 at 1.77 times the speed. The findings show that the input representation can be an important source of efficiency. In this setting, computation can benefit from information already available within the image codec.
neurips-2018-faster-neural-networks-stra.tldr: Training adapted CNNs directly on JPEG frequency coefficients produces ImageNet models with improved speed, including 1.77× speed at similar ResNet-50 accuracy.

paragraphs: Feature hashing compresses a high-dimensional vector into a much smaller one using a very sparse random projection. Each original coordinate contributes to one output coordinate with a random positive or negative sign. The central question is how much this inexpensive transformation changes the vector’s squared Euclidean length, and how reliably that change can be controlled.

The answer depends on four quantities: the largest coordinate relative to the vector’s length, the compressed dimension, the tolerated relative error, and the allowed failure probability. Earlier results gave sufficient conditions connecting these quantities, but left their precise tradeoff unresolved. This paper supplies tight asymptotic bounds describing that tradeoff.

The result clarifies the performance of feature hashing by connecting properties of the input vector to the compression size needed for a desired accuracy and reliability. The authors also compare the theory with empirical data. Those observations indicate that the constants hidden in the asymptotic bounds are close to one, supporting the practical tightness of the analysis in the examined settings.
neurips-2018-fully-understanding-the-has.tldr: Tight asymptotic bounds characterize how feature hashing trades compressed dimension and input concentration against norm-preservation accuracy and failure probability.

paragraphs: The paper studies faster computation of a real symmetric matrix’s leading eigenvector. It focuses on shift-and-invert preconditioning, an acceleration technique whose practical appeal has grown with fast least-squares solvers that approximate the matrix inversions used in power iterations. The authors examine this technique through the perspective of inexact Riemannian gradient descent.

That perspective makes the choice of step size central. The shifted-and-inverted power method appears as a special case with adaptive step sizes. The paper then studies constant step sizes and Barzilai-Borwein step sizes, using theoretical analysis, experiments, or both. This connects a familiar eigenvector procedure to a broader set of optimization choices.

For constant step sizes, the authors prove a convergence rate of approximately the square root of λ₁ divided by λ₁ − λₚ₊₁, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here p is the multiplicity of the largest eigenvalue, so the expression accounts for repeated leading eigenvalues. Experiments show that the proposed algorithm can be significantly faster than the shifted-and-inverted power method in practice.
neurips-2018-gradient-descent-meets-shif.tldr: Viewing shift-and-invert eigenvector computation as gradient descent reveals useful step-size choices, with convergence analysis and empirical speed gains.

paragraphs: This paper examines how cooperation can develop in social dilemmas that unfold across time and space. Such settings are more complex than a single matrix game because actions influence later situations and rewards. The authors focus on inequity aversion: a preference against unequal outcomes that is present in many, though not all, people.

The work extends this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning in Markov games. In simpler social-dilemma models, inequity-averse individuals can support cooperation through prosocial behavior and punishment of defectors. Here, the authors investigate how the same kind of preference interacts with the process by which agents learn policies in sequential environments.

They find that inequity aversion promotes cooperation in several types of sequential social dilemma through its interaction with policy learnability. In intertemporal social dilemmas specifically, it improves temporal credit assignment, helping connect consequences across time to the behavior that produced them. These findings offer a possible explanation for how cooperation can emerge and persist at larger scales, grounded in both social preferences and learning dynamics.
neurips-2018-inequity-aversion-improves-.tldr: Inequity-averse preferences promote cooperation in several sequential social dilemmas, partly by improving temporal credit assignment.

paragraphs: The paper addresses two connected audio problems: separating several sound sources from microphone recordings and estimating where those sources are located. It treats these as a joint inference task. The observations used by the model are differences in sound phase between microphones, which provide information relevant to the spatial organization of the recorded sources.

Inspired by topic models, the authors construct a probabilistic model and formulate separation and localization as Bayesian inference. The approach assumes that sound activity varies smoothly within local neighborhoods of time, frequency, and location. It also uses the known microphone positions to obtain a consistent separation, linking statistical structure in the audio to the recording geometry.

The authors compare their method with existing algorithms using simulated voice recordings in anechoic conditions, where reverberation is absent. They report high performance across a variety of input conditions. The evidence therefore supports the joint modeling approach in the evaluated simulated setting, with local smoothness and known microphone positions serving as explicit ingredients of the method.
neurips-2018-latent-gaussian-activity-pr.tldr: A Bayesian model combines microphone phase differences, known positions, and local activity smoothness to jointly separate and locate sound sources.

paragraphs: The paper explores whether a model’s training objective should change as learning progresses. In conventional training, the loss function is specified in advance and remains fixed. Here, a second model acts as a teacher by producing loss functions for a student model at different training stages. The teacher’s goal is to improve the student’s performance on a development dataset.

This setup makes the learning objective itself an output of a trainable system. The teacher is a parametric model whose choices shape what the student optimizes over time. The authors develop an efficient way to train the teacher with gradient-based optimization, avoiding the policy-optimization approach described as ineffective for this purpose.

The resulting method, L2T-DLF, is evaluated on real-world tasks including image classification and neural machine translation. Extensive experiments show significant improvements in the quality of various student models. These findings support dynamically learned loss functions as a useful way to guide training, with success measured by the student’s development performance rather than simply by its progress on a fixed training objective.
neurips-2018-learning-to-teach-with-dyna.tldr: A trainable teacher dynamically supplies student loss functions, improving tested image-classification and translation models through gradient-based teacher learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies selecting k items to maximize the weakest of several monotone submodular objectives. These objectives reward adding items but exhibit diminishing returns. Although greedy methods work well for one objective, balancing many objectives is harder. The number of objectives, m, is crucial: the abstract identifies inapproximability when m grows on the order of k, unless P equals NP.

The authors extend approximation guarantees beyond a constant number of objectives. Their modified algorithm achieves a 1 − 1/e approximation when m is little-o of k divided by log³ k. They also develop a faster randomized approach using multiplicative weight updates, obtaining an asymptotic approximation of (1 − 1/e)² − δ in roughly n/δ³ time, with logarithmic factors suppressed.

A deterministic alternative achieves a (1 − 1/e) − ε approximation, with runtime kn raised to m/ε⁴. Together, the results expose tradeoffs among speed, approximation quality, and the number of objectives. Synthetic experiments on Kronecker graphs also show that a heuristic inspired by the multiplicative-weight approach outperforms existing heuristics in those tests.
neurips-2018-multi-objective-maximizatio.tldr: New algorithms extend multi-objective submodular approximation guarantees beyond constant objective counts and offer a faster multiplicative-weight approach.

paragraphs: NAIS-Net builds very deep neural networks from processing blocks derived from dynamical systems. Each block repeatedly receives its original input through skip connections to its unrolled stages. This non-autonomous construction allows the authors to enforce stability while adapting the processing depth to the particular input pattern.

The architecture produces nontrivial Lipschitz input-output maps even when a block is unrolled indefinitely. Such maps control how strongly outputs change in response to input changes. The authors prove global asymptotic stability, with exactly one input-dependent equilibrium for every initial condition when tanh units are used. With rectified linear units, the framework allows multiple stable equilibria.

The paper also presents an efficient implementation that enforces the derived stability conditions for fully connected and convolutional layers. Experiments demonstrate stable behavior in practice and a significant reduction in the generalization gap compared with ResNets. The contribution connects architectural design, mathematical stability, and observed generalization behavior, while explicitly distinguishing the equilibrium behavior of the two activation types.
neurips-2018-nais-net-stable-deep-networ.tldr: NAIS-Net uses input-connected dynamical blocks to enforce stability, support adaptive depth, and reduce the observed generalization gap relative to ResNets.

paragraphs: This paper develops two algorithms for a class of constrained convex optimization problems whose objectives may be nonsmooth. The methods combine augmented Lagrangians, alternating or linearized updates, Nesterov acceleration, and adaptive parameter selection. Their acceleration acts on the primal variables, which represent the original optimization choices, rather than on dual variables as in several earlier methods.

The main guarantees are non-ergodic: the convergence rates concern the produced iterates rather than relying on averaged iterates. Under standard assumptions, the algorithms achieve an optimal O(1/k) rate without requiring smoothness or strong convexity. With semi-strong convexity, the rate improves to O(1/k²), where k counts iterations. The faster rate therefore depends on additional problem structure.

The authors report per-iteration computational costs that match or improve upon existing algorithms, alongside the possibility of parallel implementation. Parameters are updated adaptively without heuristic tuning. Numerical examples compare the methods with state-of-the-art alternatives. Together, these features aim to make the theoretical convergence guarantees compatible with manageable iteration costs and practical parameter selection.
neurips-2018-non-ergodic-alternating-pro.tldr: Two adaptive constrained-optimization algorithms achieve optimal non-averaged convergence rates, including O(1/k²) under semi-strong convexity.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision-making when a Markov decision process has uncertain parameters. A standard robust approach chooses a policy that maximizes expected reward against the worst permitted parameters. Common uncertainty sets describe states independently, a property called rectangularity. This makes computation tractable, but can produce overly conservative policies and hinder transfer of knowledge between states or related processes.

The authors propose non-rectangular uncertainty sets based on marginal moments of state-action features across entire trajectories. These constraints describe uncertainty using properties of the overall sequence of decisions and states. The formulation enables generalization across parts of the state space while retaining an appropriate representation of uncertainty in the decision process.

To solve the resulting robust decision problems, the authors develop algorithms that reduce them to finding an optimal policy for a mixture of decision processes. Experiments demonstrate benefits of the approach. The main contribution is therefore both representational and computational: it changes how uncertainty is expressed and supplies a way to optimize policies under that richer description.
neurips-2018-policy-conditioned-uncertai.tldr: Trajectory-level uncertainty constraints support robust policies that share information across states, with solution methods based on mixtures of decision processes.

paragraphs: The paper considers a learner trying to locate a random target within an interval by asking queries. An adversary observes every query but cannot see the responses. The learner must therefore gain enough information to estimate the target accurately while ensuring that the visible query sequence does not reveal too much about its location.

The privacy requirement is expressed through a parameter L: no adversary estimator should achieve a constant additive error with probability greater than 1/L. The learner’s own desired error is ε. The authors establish a lower bound that is tight to first order, showing query complexity on the order of L log(1/ε) as ε approaches zero.

The result identifies a multiplicative privacy cost in this setting. Increasing L strengthens the restriction on an adversary’s success, but multiplies the number of queries needed at the leading order. The proof uses Fano’s inequality and properties of proportional-sampling estimators. Its significance is a quantitative connection between accurate learning and concealment when the learner’s questions themselves are observable.
neurips-2018-query-complexity-of-bayesia.tldr: When an adversary sees queries but not answers, stronger target privacy incurs a multiplicative query cost of order L log(1/ε).

paragraphs: RetGK addresses how to measure similarity between graphs. This is a foundational problem when data are represented by connected entities, as in computer vision, bioinformatics, and social networks. The paper develops graph kernels, which provide similarity measures that can be used for tasks such as assigning whole graphs to categories.

The framework bases those kernels on the probabilities that random walks return to their starting nodes. This connects the similarity measure to how movement through a graph reflects its structure. The proposed kernels can also exploit different kinds of node attributes, allowing information attached to individual nodes to contribute alongside the graph’s connectivity. Scalability to large datasets is another stated advantage.

The authors evaluate their kernels through extensive graph classification experiments. They report significantly better accuracy and computational efficiency than other state-of-the-art approaches in those comparisons. The findings support return probabilities as a useful basis for graph comparison, with the tested framework combining structural information, node attributes, and efficient computation.
neurips-2018-retgk-graph-kernels-based-o.tldr: RetGK compares graphs through random-walk return probabilities and node attributes, improving classification accuracy and computational efficiency in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper focuses on primary multi-task learning, where auxiliary tasks are used to improve one task of central interest. Its main contribution is ROCK, a generic block for combining multiple kinds of representations in a deep network. The architecture is designed around the question of how auxiliary predictions can directly help the primary prediction.

ROCK uses a residual connection so that intermediate auxiliary representations explicitly affect the forward prediction. The auxiliary predictor also uses intensive pooling operations intended to make its intermediate representations more complementary. This gives the supporting tasks a concrete architectural route into the primary task, alongside their role in training the network.

Experiments on NYUv2 use object detection as the primary task, supported by scene classification, depth prediction, and surface normal estimation. The authors report improvements over flat multi-task approaches and a large margin over state-of-the-art object detectors on that dataset. The method also handles large-scale mixtures of real and synthetic images when some annotation modalities are missing, supporting its use with heterogeneous training inputs.
neurips-2018-revisiting-multi-task-learn.tldr: ROCK feeds auxiliary-task representations into primary predictions through a residual fusion block, improving object detection on NYUv2.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to determine whether the smallest mean among a finite collection of distributions lies above or below a threshold. Samples are gathered sequentially, so the method must decide which distribution to observe next and when enough evidence has accumulated. This question arises as a subproblem in planning, game-tree search, and reinforcement learning.

Refined finite-sample lower bounds show that optimal sampling behavior differs substantially depending on whether the true minimum is low or high. Thompson Sampling and a Lower Confidence Bounds policy each handle only one of these cases optimally. The authors introduce Murphy Sampling, which considers exclusively low-minimum possibilities yet is proved optimal for both outcomes.

The paper also develops self-normalized deviation inequalities that support more aggressive stopping rules. These rules concern when the accumulated observations justify ending the test, complementing the choice of what to sample. Experiments show Murphy Sampling performing best in the tested comparisons. The contribution combines an explanation of the task’s asymmetric demands with a method that addresses both sides.
neurips-2018-sequential-test-for-the-low.tldr: Murphy Sampling optimally tests whether a collection’s lowest mean crosses a threshold, handling two cases that challenge standard sampling policies differently.

paragraphs: This paper examines the statistical and computational requirements of kernel principal component analysis when it is implemented using random Fourier features. The feature representation makes the number of features a central computational choice. The authors ask how large that representation needs to be to achieve a specified sample-complexity rate.

Their result shows that, under mild assumptions, O(√n log n) random features suffice to achieve O(1/ε²) sample complexity. The feature count grows roughly with the square root of n, with an additional logarithmic factor. This is a sufficiency result: it establishes that the stated number is enough under the assumptions, rather than claiming that every successful method must use that many features.

The authors also provide a memory-efficient streaming algorithm based on classical Oja’s algorithm and show that it achieves the same rate. Streaming makes the result relevant to processing observations as they arrive. Together, the analysis and algorithm connect an economical feature representation with a procedure that retains the stated statistical performance while using memory efficiently.
neurips-2018-streaming-kernel-pca-with-t.tldr: Under mild assumptions, O(√n log n) random features suffice for the stated kernel-PCA sample rate, achieved by a memory-efficient streaming algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies recommendation through natural conversation, where a focused goal can develop into more open-ended discussion. It contributes ReDial, a publicly released dataset of more than 10,000 conversations about movie recommendations. The dataset provides a shared resource for investigating how recommendation and dialogue interact in conversations centered on this task.

The authors use ReDial to explore neural architectures, mechanisms, and methods for conversational recommendation systems. They examine components addressing different parts of the problem, including sentiment analysis, recommendation generation in cold-start settings, and the ways people use natural language during recommendation exchanges. This supports systematic study of the pieces needed to sustain a useful recommendation conversation.

The work then combines these components into a complete dialogue system and examines its behavior. Its contribution is both a research dataset and an exploration of system composition. By bringing recommendation, interpretation of preferences, and language interaction into one setting, the paper creates a basis for studying how those capabilities work together.
neurips-2018-towards-deep-conversational.tldr: ReDial supplies over 10,000 movie-recommendation conversations and supports exploration of neural components combined into a conversational recommender.

paragraphs: This paper develops an agent that practices reaching goals before knowing which goals a user will request at test time. The challenge is to acquire broadly useful skills directly from visual observations. The proposed method combines unsupervised representation learning with reinforcement learning of policies whose behavior is conditioned on a goal.

During a self-supervised practice phase, the agent imagines goals and attempts to reach them. Its learned visual representation serves three roles: generating practice goals, transforming raw sensory inputs into a structured representation, and computing rewards for goal achievement. This makes representation learning part of both the agent’s perception and the process that supplies its training objectives.

The authors also introduce retroactive goal relabeling to improve sample efficiency by changing how past experience is associated with goals. Their off-policy algorithm is efficient enough to learn from raw image observations and image goals in a real physical system. It substantially outperforms prior techniques in the reported evaluation, supporting self-directed visual practice as a route to reusable goal-reaching skills.
neurips-2018-visual-reinforcement-learni.tldr: An agent learns visual goal-reaching skills through imagined practice goals, a shared learned representation, and retroactive goal relabeling.

paragraphs: The paper experimentally investigates why strong image classifiers can also be vulnerable to adversarial changes. Its central finding connects the two behaviors: the image-space directions that contribute to classification performance are also directions along which the examined networks are especially vulnerable. This links successful prediction and adversarial sensitivity through the same aspects of the input.

The analysis proceeds in two steps. First, the authors show that classes tend to be associated with particular directions in image space. They examine how class scores change as an input moves along one such direction at a time. This viewpoint also offers an explanation of universal adversarial perturbations through the directional structure of class responses.

Second, the authors demonstrate a tight relationship between classification performance and attack vulnerability within spaces spanned by these directions. The finding explains how accuracy and vulnerability can coexist in the studied networks. It also gives efforts to improve robustness a specific relationship to consider: changes to sensitivity in these spaces interact with information the classifier uses for prediction.
neurips-2018-with-friends-like-these-who.tldr: Experiments link adversarial vulnerability to the same image-space directions that support classification performance in deep convolutional networks.
